sec.title: 5.4. Illustrative Application of the Δ Architecture: English Regular Plural
sec.p: The preceding section described the regular English plural within Distributed Morphology. The present section applies the Δ architecture separately to the relation cat → cats at the selected executional level; it does not reproduce the morphological or phonological derivation.
At the macrostructural level, the relation is formalized as: A Δ (+n) = A′. Here, A identifies the initial nominal configuration, n the dependent plural material, and A′ the resulting configuration.

At the microstructural level, the corresponding integration is represented as: 1C [(R 0 +)] + c [(R 0 )+] = 2C [(R 0 +)]. Here, R 0 remains constant, while c [(R 0 )+] identifies the integrated dependent plural component. The formulas represent the same executional intervention at coordinated levels of analysis.

This application has a deliberately narrow scope: Distributed Morphology explains how the regular plural exponent is inserted and subsequently realized phonologically. The Δ classification complements that account without replacing it.

The example also illustrates why regime assignment requires a specified representational level: the present analysis concerns morphological execution, not the phonological surface alternation. The status and executional classification of the English relation cat → cats are documented in Appendix B, Figure 4, “Status and Selection of Illustrative Configurations.”

sec.title: 6. Formal Constraints and Conditions of Revision
sec.p: The Δ operatorial architecture establishes internal constraints for the classification of transformational interventions. These constraints derive from the unicity of Δ, the macro-micro distinction, and the activation criteria of the regimes. They govern regime assignment once the representational level and structural type of intervention have been identified; they do not constitute claims about all linguistic systems. The following subsections specify the relevant constraints, conditions of applicability, and conditions of revision.

sec.title: 6.1. Hypothesis of Unique Regime Assignment at the Same Representational Level
sec.p: Once its representational level has been specified, a transformational intervention receives one operatorial regime assignment at that level. This hypothesis does not require that a phenomenon receive only one description across all levels of analysis. For example, Δ (→) may record an oriented correspondence at the relational level, while Δ (−/+) classifies substitution at the executional level in a separate representation. These are complementary descriptions, not competing assignments within one formula.

The hypothesis requires revision if a clearly specified intervention satisfies the defining conditions of two competing regimes at the same representational level. A difference between relational and executional descriptions at distinct levels does not constitute such a case.
The single-regime condition and its level-specific qualification are summarized in Appendix B, Figure 3, “Decision Rules for Regime Assignment.”

sec.title: 6.2. Macro-Micro Correspondence Constraint
sec.p: This internal constraint applies whenever the analysis claims an executional intervention within a configuration. The macrostructural formula identifies the type of intervention and the dependent material involved, whereas the microstructural formula specifies the corresponding component, its position relative to R 0 , and the resulting internally organized configuration. For example, an additive relation represented at the macrostructural level as A Δ (+n) = A′ requires a microstructural representation that identifies the integrated component c and its relation to R 0 .

The constraint does not require relational formulas, such as Δ (→), to duplicate an executional analysis when no internal material operation is claimed. It requires only that an intervention described as executional at the macrostructural level have a compatible microstructural representation, and that an internal executional modification be expressible through a stabilized macrostructural relation.

An incompatible observation would be a proposed executional classification whose macrostructural and microstructural formulas cannot be coordinated without changing the identified intervention or redefining the relevant components. In that case, the formula, the classification, or the macro-micro correspondence rule requires revision.
The macrostructural and microstructural correspondence of the eight regimes is summarized in Appendix B, Figure 5, “Summary of the Eight Operatorial Regimes.”

sec.title: 6.3. R 0 Continuity Constraint
sec.p: This internal constraint applies to relations analyzed within a single operatorial cycle. Where the intervention concerns dependent material while the relational nucleus R 0 remains identifiable, the relation may be represented through the applicable operatorial regime at the specified representational level. The continuity of R 0 is therefore a condition for treating the result as a modified realization of the same configuration.

The constraint does not state that every formal difference preserves R 0 . When the diagnostic established in Section 3.6 shows that no common relational nucleus can be retained without an unmotivated redefinition, the resulting form is treated as a distinct configuration requiring a new R 0 and the initiation of a new operatorial cycle.

An incompatible observation would be a relation in which R 0 must be reidentified while the architecture nevertheless classifies the change as an internal executional intervention within the same cycle. Such a case requires revision of the R 0 diagnostic, the proposed classification, or the rule governing the initiation of a new operatorial cycle.
The diagnostic for retaining or replacing R 0 is set out in Appendix B, Figure 2, “Decision Procedure for Retaining or Replacing R 0 .”

sec.title: 6.4. Activation Threshold Constraint, Δ (±)
sec.p: This internal constraint applies to the cumulative paradigmatic flexibility regime Δ (±). The regime is activated only where a structured paradigmatic domain contains at least three correlated and structurally analysable realizations sharing the same R 0 . The threshold k ≥ 3 is a formal convention of the present architecture, not a universal empirical limit. Its function is to distinguish a paradigmatic domain from an isolated transformation or binary alternation, which require analysis through the specific local intervention involved.

For the purposes of this constraint, k counts the distinct structurally analysable realizations that constitute the correlated paradigmatic domain. The identification of such realizations is therefore determined by their formal representation within the architecture rather than by the mere number of paradigmatic positions considered.

An incompatible observation would be a proposed Δ (±) domain containing fewer than three correlated realizations or lacking a common R 0 . Such a case requires reclassification as a local intervention or revision of the threshold convention.
The activation threshold for Δ (±) and its exclusion of isolated or binary relations are summarized in Appendix B, Figure 5, “Summary of the Eight Operatorial Regimes.”

sec.title: 6.5. Relational Non-Interference Constraint, Δ (>/<)
sec.p: This internal constraint applies where Δ (>/<) is used to describe the stabilization of a functional relation between already constituted units. In a single relational formula, the regime does not classify the integration, elimination, substitution, or positional reorganization of the internal material of those units. Such material interventions require an executional regime.

The constraint does not prohibit a phenomenon from receiving both a relational and an executional description at different representational levels. It requires only that Δ (>/<) not be combined with an executional regime as competing classifications of the same formula and at the same level of representation.

An incompatible observation would be a formula in which Δ (>/<) is assigned to a relation while the same formula also claims an internal material intervention without distinguishing a separate executional representation. Such a case requires revision of the formula or of the assigned regime. The non-interference of relational coupling and executional classifications at the same representational level is summarized in Appendix B, Figure 3, “Decision Rules for Regime Assignment.”

sec.title: 6.6. Conditions for Cross-Linguistic Applicability
sec.p: The Δ architecture proposes that its regime definitions may be applied comparatively to structurally described interventions in different languages. This is a proposed condition of applicability, not an established claim of cross-linguistic stability. The selected examples show only that the proposed criteria can be used within a limited illustrative dataset.

Cross-linguistic applicability requires further assessment with typologically broader data and independent analyses. A relevant challenge would arise if structurally comparable interventions, described at the same representational level, repeatedly required incompatible regime assignments solely because of language-specific structural properties. Such a result would require revision of the relevant activation criterion, the level distinction, or the proposed inventory of regimes.
The languages and illustrative configurations included in this limited dataset are documented in Appendix B, Figure 4, “Status and Selection of Illustrative Configurations.”

sec.title: 6.7. Conditions of Revision
sec.p: Revision is required when a phenomenon cannot be assigned to a regime under the stated criteria or when the unique-regime condition specified in Section 6.1 fails; the relevant activation condition, level distinction, or regime inventory must then be reconsidered. The absence of an identified case requiring revision does not confirm the model; further independent applications are needed to assess the scope and consistency of the proposed classifications.

sec.title: 6.8. Structural Exclusions and Conditions of Revision
sec.p: The Δ operatorial architecture imposes internal limits derived from its definitions, identifying combinations that the present formal system does not classify within a single representation. This does not constitute a negative typological prediction about all languages.

At a given representational level, competing regime assignments are excluded. The specific exclusions for each regime are summarized in Sections 4.1-4.8. Complementary relational and executional descriptions remain possible only when they are stated in separate representations and concern distinct levels.

An internal executional relation requires continuity of R 0 . Where the diagnostic in Section 3.6 requires a new R 0 , the result begins a new operatorial cycle rather than constituting an internal transformation. Δ (±) applies only to a domain containing at least three correlated realizations, as specified in Section 6.4. Δ (>/<) applies only where no internal material intervention is claimed in the same formula; an intervention affecting material requires a separate executional representation. A configuration that cannot be treated under these conditions invokes the revision procedure specified in Section 6.7.

sec.title: 6.9. Boundary Cases and Conditions of Revision
sec.p: The examples go → went and la ~ al mark distinct limits of the present architecture. In go → went, no common R 0 can be retained without redefining the lexical relation. The result is therefore treated as the beginning of a new operatorial cycle rather than as an internal executional transformation.
he diagnostic governing this result is set out in Appendix B, Figure 2, “Decision Procedure for Retaining or Replacing R 0 .”

The constructed correspondence la ~ al visualizes the formal possibility of positional permutation, but it does not establish an attested derivational, synchronic, or historical relation in Romanian. It cannot support a linguistic classification through Δ (~) unless continuity of R 0 and preservation of the material inventory are independently established. The constructed formal illustration is provided in Appendix B, Figure 13, “Visual Illustration of the Δ(~) Positional Reorganization Regime.”
These cases delimit the scope of the current criteria; if comparable attested cases cannot be treated under those conditions, the conditions of revision specified in Section 6.7 apply.

sec.title: 7. Extended Case Study: urs → ursoaică
sec.p: This section applies the analytical protocol to the Romanian relation urs → ursoaică ([ 19 ]) as a boundary case for the proposed architecture. The relation involves suffixal dependent material directionally related to an identifiable lexical base and an associated semantic and grammatical reorientation. It therefore tests whether Δ (><) can classify the directional relation between dependent material and a lexical configuration while R 0 remains identifiable.

The analysis treats the relation at two distinct representational levels. At the executional level, the suffixal material -oaică is integrated into the lexical base urs and is classified through Δ (+). At the semantic-relational level, the suffixal material is directionally related to the base and produces an explicitly identifiable feminine lexical and grammatical reorientation; this relation is classified through Δ (><). These are complementary classifications at distinct levels, not competing assignments within one representation. The analysis therefore tests the activation conditions of both regimes and the retention of R 0 . The source, status, and dual-level classification of the relation urs → ursoaică are documented in Appendix B, Figure 4, “Status and Selection of Illustrative Configurations.”

Three stages organize the case study: description of the empirical relation and its structural segmentation; comparison with the explanatory perspectives of selected theoretical frameworks; and formalization within the Δ architecture. Unless a source is cited for a specific analysis of this exact relation, framework-specific characterizations are comparative reconstructions based on the general commitments of the respective approaches.

sec.title: 7.1. The Empirical Phenomenon
sec.p: The Romanian relation urs → ursoaică is examined as a case in which suffixal dependent material is directionally related to a lexical base and produces a semantic and grammatical reorientation. Urs denotes a male bear, whereas ursoaică denotes a female bear. For the purposes of the present analysis, the base urs remains identifiable in the resulting form, while the sequence -oaică constitutes dependent material absent from the initial configuration. The source, gloss, and analytical classification of this example are provided in Appendix B4, “Status and Selection of Illustrative Configurations.”

The presence of the suffixal material -oaică supports an executional classification through Δ (+), because the material is integrated into the lexical base urs without the elimination or replacement of pre-existing material. At the semantic-relational level, the suffixal material is directionally related to the lexical base and produces a stabilized feminine lexical and grammatical reorientation; this relation is classified through Δ (><), subject to the R 0 diagnostic established in Section 3.6.

sec.title: 7.2. Cross-Framework Interpretation and Instability
sec.p: The following discussion presents comparative reconstructions based on the general theoretical commitments of Minimalism, Distributed Morphology, and Word-and-Paradigm morphology. It does not attribute a published framework-specific analysis of the Romanian relation urs → ursoaică to these approaches.

These perspectives may assign different descriptive statuses to the same empirical relation, but their differences are not necessarily limited to the location of explanation. They may also involve different assumptions about the representation, realization, and organization of grammatical information. The comparison therefore does not establish that the empirical structure is independent of theoretical analysis. It identifies the need for a separate comparative description of the formally specified relation. Within the Δ architecture, that description distinguishes two representational levels: Δ (+) classifies the integration of the suffixal material at the executional level, whereas Δ (><) classifies the associated directional semantic and grammatical reorientation at the semantic- relational level.

sec.title: 7.3. Formalization in the Δ Architecture
sec.p: The Romanian relation urs → ursoaică receives complementary classifications at two distinct representational levels. At the executional level, the suffixal material -oaică is integrated into the lexical base urs and is classified through Δ (+). At the semantic-relational level, that suffixal material is directionally related to the lexical base and produces an explicitly identified feminine lexical and grammatical reorientation; this relation is classified through Δ (><).

At the executional level, the macrostructural relation is represented as: A + n = A′. Here, A designates urs, n designates the integrated suffixal material -oaică, and A′ designates ursoaică. The formula represents the integration of dependent material through Δ (+).

At the microstructural level, the corresponding relation is represented as: 1C [(R 0 +)] + c [(R 0 )+] = 2C [(R 0 +)]. Here, 1C [(R 0 +)] identifies the configuration associated with urs, c [(R 0 )+] identifies the suffixal dependent material -oaică, and 2C [(R 0 +)] identifies the resulting configuration ursoaică. R 0 remains identifiable throughout the executional integration.

At the semantic-relational level, the macrostructural relation is represented as: (n > A) = B. Here, n designates the dependent suffixal material -oaică, A designates urs, and B designates ursoaică. The formula records the directional relation of n to A and the resulting stabilized configuration.

At the microstructural level, the corresponding relation is represented as: c [(R 0 )+] > C1 [(R 0 +)] = C2 [(R 0 +)]. Here, c [(R 0 )+] represents the suffixal component -oaică, C1 [(R 0 +)] identifies the configuration associated with urs, and C2 [(R 0 +)] identifies the resulting configuration ursoaică. The marker > specifies the directional relation of the suffixal component to the configuration relative to R 0 . It does not constitute an independent operator; Δ (><) remains the semantic-relational classification.

The analysis is maintained only if the diagnostic in Section 3.6 permits the relational nucleus associated with urs to be retained. Any framework-specific explanation of feminine lexical or grammatical value remains distinct from this comparative description.

sec.title: 7.4. Regime Stability and Theoretical Consequence
sec.p: The Δ architecture permits complementary classifications of a single relation when they apply at distinct representational levels and are stated in separate representations. Each classification must satisfy its own activation condition, and the analysis must meet the R 0 -continuity diagnostic in Section 3.6.

The example remains illustrative: it neither establishes invariant classification across theoretical frameworks nor supports a universally applicable criterion. Broader empirical testing and independent analyses are needed to determine whether the distinction extends to other configurations.

sec.title: 8. Discussion and Theoretical Implications
sec.p: The Δ operatorial architecture provides a formal framework for comparing grammatical transformations by distinguishing the structural type of an intervention from the framework-specific mechanisms used to explain it. Minimalist, Distributed Morphology, Word-and-Paradigm, and Construction Grammar accounts may locate explanation in different components of grammar; the architecture neither replaces these accounts nor determines which is correct. Its narrower purpose is to classify structurally specified relations as oriented correspondence, integration, elimination, correlated replacement, semantic or grammatical reorientation, relational coupling, positional reorganization, or paradigmatic organization.

This comparative function depends on the distinction between macrostructural and microstructural representation: macrostructural formulas record stabilized relations between configurations, while microstructural formulas specify R 0 and the dependent material affected. Thus, Δ (→) can record the oriented correspondence between casă and case without classifying their internal material change; that executional replacement of -ă by -e is classified separately as Δ (−/+). Similarly, Δ (+) classifies material integration, while Δ (><) may classify the resulting semantic-relational reorientation in a separate representation. In trust → distrust and urs → ursoaică, these classifications are complementary because they apply at distinct representational levels.

The eight regimes form a proposed inventory, not an exhaustive typology. Uncertain identification of R 0 , multiple exponence, conversion, suppletion, syncretism, overabundance, and non-concatenative morphology may require revising an activation criterion, reconsidering the representational level, or modifying the inventory. The architecture’s specific contribution is a comparative vocabulary for structural interventions, coordinated macro-micro notation, and an explicit procedure for assigning regimes. Appendix B, Figure 5, “Summary of the Eight Operatorial Regimes,” presents the inventory and its macrostructural and microstructural representations.

sec.title: 9. Scope and Limitations
sec.p: The Δ operatorial architecture is proposed as a formal comparative framework for classifying transformational interventions. Its scope is therefore limited: it does not offer a complete account of how grammatical structures are generated or model cognitive processing, language acquisition, historical development, or the mechanisms through which speakers construct linguistic expressions. Those explanatory questions remain within the remit of generative, realizational, paradigmatic, phonological, and constructional frameworks. The architecture is neither a psychological entity nor an independently demonstrated universal principle; it applies only when a relation can be represented through the proposed macrostructural and microstructural notation. Because classification depends on the representational level selected and on identifying a regime’s defining condition, each level receives a single regime assignment. Complementary descriptions are possible only in separate representations at distinct levels.

A further limitation concerns the identification of R 0 . The ordered diagnostic specifies when the relational nucleus should be retained or replaced, but applying it may be difficult when more than one candidate base configuration is plausible. The procedure is presented in Appendix B2, “Decision Procedure for Retaining or Replacing R 0 .” Since this study includes no independent coding or assessment of inter-analyst agreement, it does not claim that the diagnostic has been independently validated. Future research should develop a coding manual for the operatorial regimes and assess whether independent analysts assign the same regime when they apply the diagnostic to the same data.

The attested dataset is illustrative and selective, so it does not establish typological coverage or cross-linguistic stability. Phenomena such as multiple exponence, conversion, extensive syncretism, overabundance, non-concatenative morphology, polysynthesis, and gradient alternations may require refinement of an activation criterion, reconsideration of the representational level, or revision of the inventory. Likewise, the threshold k ≥ 3 for Δ (±) is a formal convention for distinguishing a paradigmatic domain from an isolated transformation or binary alternation; it is not proposed as a universal threshold. Its conditions and exclusions are summarized in Appendix B5, “Summary of the Eight Operatorial Regimes.” The architecture remains open to revision if a clearly specified intervention cannot be classified under the stated criteria or requires two competing regime assignments at the same representational level.

sec.title: 10. Conclusion
sec.p: This paper has proposed the Δ operatorial architecture as a formal means of comparing grammatical transformations. It treats transformation as a structurally identifiable intervention and keeps its classification distinct from the mechanism a particular theory invokes to explain it. The general operator Δ organizes this comparative description: macrostructural formulas record stabilized relations between configurations, while microstructural formulas specify R 0 and the dependent components affected. The architecture thus allows different theoretical accounts to be compared without replacing them or deciding which is empirically correct.

This formal approach does not require one fully specified formula that applies at both representational levels or to every relation. Each formula is selected for a particular relation and identifies its configurations, orientation, relevant material, or Δ regime. Generality resides in the operatorial architecture, its regimes, and the conditions for applying them—not in a universal formula. Formulas are not created ex nihilo; they are selected and specified by applying pre-established classificatory conditions.

A limited comparison with mathematical formalization helps clarify this order of analysis. A general mathematical equation or formula normally precedes the assignment of values to its variables; in the Δ architecture, the structural relation is identified before its formal representation is selected. Since surface form alone is insufficient for structural classification, the analysis must establish the relation between configurations and determine the applicable regime. The comparison does not make Δ a mathematical model: the architecture describes structural relations formally but does not explain their cognitive, historical, or causal origins.

The examples offer a preliminary illustration of the proposed criteria, not evidence of an exhaustive typology or universal classificatory stability. The proposal remains open to revision if an intervention cannot be classified under the stated conditions, R 0 cannot be identified consistently, or two competing regimes are required at the same representational level. Its broader applicability therefore requires further empirical testing and independent analysis.
“A word becomes truly alive only when it can become something else without ceasing to be itself.”
Ciocioc Ion Valentin
